How does gender affect the effectiveness of public sector interventions? Evidence for Colombia
https://www.nesta.org.uk/blog/how-gender-affects-effectiveness-public-sector-interventions/
Author: Hannah Ritchie, Hannah Ritchie, Nesta
Colombia has one of the highest per capita levels of violence. Homicides and femicides are especially prevalent. An estimated 60,000 people are estimated to have died violently annually from 2000 to 2011.
The public sector spends a lot of money on violence prevention, including programs aimed specifically at women and girls. But what about programmes intended for men, or which affect men in some way?
Nesta is starting a new research partnership with the World Bank, working in conjunction with researchers from the University of Sydney and Johns Hopkins University. The research project will assess the effectiveness of interventions in Colombia designed to lower levels of domestic violence and femicide.
Many public interventions have assumed that men are the key drivers of gender inequality, and that targeted interventions should be directed primarily at men. This assumption is commonly termed the "gender equality-effectiveness hypothesis" (EEH). In other words, the hope is that if you reach out to men and teach them skills in communication, self-control and non-violent coping mechanisms you will see lower rates of gender-based violence among the men who have been reached.
But is it true that programmes specifically targeted to men can have an effect on gender-based violence? Do programmes that include men get the same gains that gender-only programmes do?
If the EEH is true, then public policies which include men will reduce rates of gender-based violence (GBV) as much as public policies which have no men as part of them. In that case, we would expect to see a decrease in gender-based violence in areas with lots of men-targeted programmes.
In areas with no men-targeted programmes, we would expect no decrease in gender-based violence.
If, on the other hand, specific programmes for men are much less effective than gender-only programmes, then we would expect we would see a decrease in gender-based violence and homicide wherever any programme is being implemented.
This seems like a reasonable hypothesis to test. Public policies that specifically involve men should be no more effective than public policies that include men but no explicit focus
